text.p: Following are some of the major events to have occurred on July 21 in history:
1403 - The Percy family rebelled against King Henry IV at Shrewsbury. Henry Percy, better known as Harry Hotspur, was killed in the battle.
1542 - In a strengthening of the fight against Protestantism, Pope Paul III set up an inquisition.
1718 - The Peace of Passarowitz was signed, ending the wars between Austria and Turkey and Venice and Turkey.
1773 - Pope Clement XIV issues the Papal bull "Dominus ac Redemptor" dissolving the Jesuit Order
1796 - Robert Burns, Scottish national poet and composer of songs and airs, died.
1798 - The Battle of the Pyramids took place in Egypt. The Mameluke army tried to stop Napoleon's march on Cairo but were repulsed and eventually driven into the Nile, where many drowned.
1816 - Paul Julius (Baron von) Reuter, founder of the news agency that bears his name, born in Germany as Israel Beer Josaphat.

1861 - In the American Civil War the Confederates routed Union forces at the first Battle of Bull Run. A key player was Thomas Jackson, described by the Union forces as standing his ground like a "stone wall" -- a nickname that stuck.
1897 - The Tate Gallery in London was opened by the Prince of Wales.
1899 - Ernest Miller Hemingway, U.S. novelist and short story writer, born. His experiences during World War One inspired him to write "A Farewell To Arms".
1904 - After 13 years, the 4,607-mile Trans-Siberian railway was completed.

1925 - The "Monkey Trial" ended in Tennessee. The state had banned the teaching of evolution in schools because it challenged the bible. John Scopes ignored the ban and taught Darwin's, theories for which he was convicted.
1926 - Karel Reisz, Czech-born film director, notably of "Saturday Night and Sunday Morning" and "Morgan: A Suitable Case For Treatment", born.
1926 - Norman Jewison, Canadian film director, born. Films include "The Thomas Crown Affair" and "Fiddler on the Roof".
1944 - U.S. forces liberated the Pacific island of Guam, held by the Japanese since December 1941.
1960 - In Sri Lanka (then Ceylon) Sirima Bandaranaike became the world's first woman prime minister, succeeding her assassinated husband Solomon.
1960 - Francis Chichester, English navigator and yachtsman, arrived in New York aboard Gypsy Moth II, having set a record of 40 days for a solo Atlantic crossing.

1967 - Basil Rathbone, South African-born English actor, died. Famed for his portrayal of Sherlock Holmes on screen, he also became the Hollywood villain in "The Adventures of Robin Hood" and "Mark of Zorro".
1967 - Albert John Luthuli, former president of the African National Congress and Nobel Peace Prize winner, died when he was hit by a train.
1973 - France began a series of nuclear test on the Muroroa Atoll in the pacific.
1974 - Greece accepted a U.N. resolution on a ceasefire in Cyprus, a day after Turkey invaded.
1976 - The British ambassador to the Irish Republic, Christopher Ewart-Biggs, was killed by a bomb placed under his car outside his home.
1978 - Juan Pereda Asbun declared himself president of Bolivia after deposing Hugo Banzer Suarez in a coup.
1983 - Martial Law was lifted in Poland. It had been imposed in December 1981 in a crackdown against Solidarity.

1988 - Baroda Airport in India was re-opened after the runway had been blocked by a damaged Boeing 737, which had been charged by a wild bull when it came in to land. The passengers survived; the bull didn't.
1990 - About 15,000 students, dissidents and civilians took part in one of the largest anti-government rallies in years
1992 - The first Egyptian-Israeli summit for six years ended in Cairo with President Mubarak agreeing to visit Israel.
1994 - After a two-month trek across Russia following his return from 20 years of exile, Alexander Solzhenitsyn arrived back in Moscow
1994 - The European Parliament narrowly approved Luxembourg Prime Minister Jacques Santer as president of the European Commission.
